extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and stylistic standards for PR/communications writing (press releases, pitches, emails, and other earned/media communications), covering research, drafting, and editing to make messages clear, concise, and audience-focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely and often
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all readers write, but all writers read. Read as much as you can by a variety of different voices and perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading broadly (fiction, memoir, genre fiction, journalism) helps you understand what entices readers and improves your own writing voice and sense of what interests audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consume deep domain knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Consume, consume, consume! Gaining a deep knowledge of the field you’re addressing is crucial for crafting impactful messages and filling gaps rather than contributing to the cacophony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stay current on news and trends in your subject area so your communications add value and context rather than repeating obvious points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research deeply then incubate ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Go hard on research and deep thinking on one day, then forget about it; when you sit down the next morning you’ll have a clear idea and focus of what to write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dedicated research/ideation time, then allow mental incubation (sleep/step-away) before drafting to clarify focus and direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with the desired outcome in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with the end in mind! Know what you want your audience to do with the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define the target action, thought, or feeling (e.g., coverage, lead generation, awareness) and choose the format and messaging to achieve that end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the topic thoroughly (past and present)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand what you are writing about — research recent news and past history, gather information from clients and external sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background research enables you to offer a fresh lens and context; this research is arguably more important than the writing itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step back and match tools to goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Think of the goals (e.g., national top-tier story vs. hyper-focused market) and then choose the best vehicle from PR, comms, and marketing toolkits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align content format, distribution channel, and messaging with the specific outcome you want.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain simply — clarity equals understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can’t say it simply, you don’t understand it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for plain-language explanations; simple wording signals genuine understanding of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichéd lead openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Never start a release, email or any other written communication with 'X is excited to announce …'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fresher, more specific ledes that convey newsworthiness rather than formulaic corporate phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use generative AI only for a first draft
rubrics_metrics.description: Sure, use generative AI — but only for the ****y first draft. The end product needs to have a voice, be interesting reading — and accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat AI output as raw material: heavily edit for voice, accuracy, and originality; verify facts and quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize brevity; avoid adverbs and passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Brevity wins every friggin time. Adverbs and passive voice are writing killers if you want people to actually absorb your content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer active verbs, concise phrasing, and cut unnecessary modifiers to increase impact and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think, write, and edit like a journalist
rubrics_metrics.description: Think like a journalist, write like a journalist, edit like a journalist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use journalistic principles (clear lede, inverted pyramid, accuracy, sourcing) to produce tight, newsworthy copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write for the audience, not internal leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Write for the audience, not the C-Suite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus messaging on the audience’s needs and interests rather than internal priorities or jargon-laden corporate language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Say it directly and with confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Say it directly and with confidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hedging and weak qualifiers; present key points clearly and assertively to build credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make external people the stars of the story
rubrics_metrics.description: The more you can make people outside of your organization the stars of your story, the stronger it will be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center customers, partners, beneficiaries, or experts to increase relatability and news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use human emotion and appropriate tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Use human emotions to grab attention: Don’t shy away from writing that evokes strong feelings; the right tone can make your message resonate deeper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select tone (humor, inspiration, urgency) aligned with the message and audience; leverage emotion responsibly to increase engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate for the audience; resist editing-by-committee
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember your audience. And have the conviction to advocate for that audience, even when leadership thinks they know better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Push back on edits that dilute clarity or usefulness; keep audience benefit central during revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep asking 'so what?' to find the core
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistently ask yourself, 'so what?' until you get to the crux of what you’re trying to say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use iterative questioning to refine the core news or argument; if you can’t answer 'so what?', rethink the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow messy first drafts and then organize
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no such thing as a perfect first draft. Start with a brain dump, let it flow and get messy, then organize main themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embrace rapid drafting to capture ideas, then edit structurally to form coherent narrative and hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write tight; avoid flowery language
rubrics_metrics.description: Write it tight. Communicators tend to favor flowery language which softens their work’s impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concise, direct phrasing to deliver clear, insightful messages for the reader's benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hook the reader with a strong first line
rubrics_metrics.description: Your first line should really hit the reader and motivate them to continue reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with news, emotion, or a compelling insight to create momentum and curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format for scanners: short blocks and signposts
rubrics_metrics.description: Short sentences and paragraphs with multiple points of entry (paragraphs, indenting, bullet points, bolding, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many readers scan; use formatting and short chunks to enable quick digestion and multiple entry points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solve problems rather than sell
rubrics_metrics.description: Solve, don’t sell, in your writing. Put yourself/company in the background; focus on audience interests, needs, and experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame content around the audience’s problem and actionable solutions rather than promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview passionate insiders to capture heart
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk to the people who are the most passionate about the subject you’re writing about to capture 'heart' into your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source vivid quotes and anecdotes from invested stakeholders to enhance authenticity and emotional connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer plain words over inflated alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t utilize 'utilize' when you can just use 'use.' Identify words that can be swapped with simpler ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose common, accessible vocabulary to improve clarity and reader friendliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t bury the lede
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t bury the lede. Get your most important information out as quickly as possible, then include supporting information and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with the most newsworthy or essential information; follow with details and background in descending importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ruthless with cutting during editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut what you’ve written in half and then halve it again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for extreme concision; remove redundant, tangential, or decorative material to sharpen the message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read content aloud to check flow and authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: I ALWAYS read content out loud as part of my approval loops to ensure it reads correctly. Especially quotes — would your CEO REALLY say that?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud reveals awkward phrasing, unnatural voice, and implausible quotes; use this to refine tone and realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use subtraction technique when editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Try removing words/sentences/paragraphs and if it doesn’t lose the overall meaning … keep it out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically delete and test whether the piece still conveys its core; prefer leaner copy when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread for style and accessible reading level
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofread for AP style and an 8th-grade reading level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply handbook style (AP) and aim for readability benchmarks to maximize clarity and journalist-friendliness (suggested GenAI prompt given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Take a break before the final read
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a break before you submit. Go for a walk, get a snack, or take an entire day if you have the time. Then reread your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fresh perspective helps spot improvements beyond grammar — better structure, clearer meaning, or stronger phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft quickly, then iterate in editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Get something on paper fast and then spend your time on editing. Add, delete, reorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate drafting (speed, capture) from polishing (structure, concision) to make editing more effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a trusted, detached reviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a trusted colleague review what you have written — particularly a colleague with no attachment to the content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External reviewers catch errors and reveal whether messaging is clear to someone not invested in the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test with an outsider for clarity and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Send the pitch to someone who has nothing to do with the client/industry to make sure it’s interesting, clear, accessible, and actionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an uninvolved reader finds it compelling and understandable, it’s likely to work with broader audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate an editor who will sharpen copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Find an editor you can count on — sometimes we need the cold hard edge of an editorial X-Acto knife to make our prose sharp!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build relationships with rigorous editors who will not be afraid to cut and improve your work for clarity and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the AIDA structure when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: AIDA: Attention (quickly), Interest, Desire, Action — get attention, establish interest, create desire, and produce an action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AIDA as a structural heuristic for pitches and persuasive communications to guide reader engagement toward a desired action.
